author: reek
body: The header fields of every kind are pipe-delimited, and a pipe cannot appear in one of them. Kind 30 is the exception, and it has to be: a source definition now carries the source, and a pipe is how this language writes a sum type. Its content is the last field, length-prefixed, and it is never split. See Definition Persistence below.

author: reek
body: A SourceDefinition used to be a POINTER: a hash, and a Perforce path where the bytes could be found. That is an index over somebody else's store, not a store, and it is the whole of the self-hosted repository gap -- the founding document proposes deleting GitHub, and we had not deleted Perforce.

author: reek
body: So it carries the bytes now. sd-content is the source itself; sd-author and sd-timestamp are the two things fact-signing-content covers that the hash does not reach, and without them a definition read back off the disk cannot be turned into the SignedFact the import gate verifies.

author: reek
body: Format: hash|path|quire|chapter|signer-fp|sig-hex|author|timestamp|len|<content>

author: reek
body: The nine header fields are pipe-delimited and none of them can contain a pipe. The content can, and does: a pipe is how this language writes a sum type, so nearly every chapter in the tree has one. Content is therefore the LAST field, it is length-prefixed, and it is never split -- the reader finds the ninth pipe and takes the next `len` characters verbatim, whatever they are. Splitting the whole line on "|" and hoping, which is what this chapter used to do to every field it had, would cut a source file to pieces at its own type declarations.

author: reek
body: A line with no ninth pipe is one of the old pointer-shaped records: it parses, and it yields empty content. Reading an old store must not fail; it must tell you honestly that the bytes were never there.

target: section:A Definition Is A Signed Fact
author: reek
body: The gate in Foreword chapter ImportGate takes a FactBundle and a TrustManifest and answers with one of seven outcomes. It has always been able to; nothing could ever reach it from the disk, because a persisted definition was not a Fact and its signature did not cover one. sign-definition signed the string "hash|path|quire|chapter" -- a sentence the gate has never heard of -- so a stored definition could not have passed gate-import even in principle.

author: reek
body: These three functions are the join. A SourceDefinition becomes the Fact its hash addresses, wearing the signature the gate checks, filed in a bundle the gate can read.

author: reek
body: The whole point, in one function: everything the disk holds, offered to the gate.

author: reek
body: The store could not answer the two questions anybody actually asks it.

author: reek
body: GIVE ME Colophon.codex. It had no way to take a name. app-scan-last takes a KIND, so it returned the last fact of kind 30 -- the last source file written, whichever chapter that happened to be -- and asked for one chapter it would hand you another. It did not fail; it answered the wrong question, which is worse.

author: reek
body: WHICH VERSION IS THE CURRENT ONE. Two editions of a file are two facts, both signed, both admitted, and nothing on the disk preferred either.

author: reek
body: Neither of those needs a supersession record to fix, and I spent a while believing they did. What they need is a KEY. A source definition already has one -- its path -- and once a fact has a key the log means what every log-structured store has always meant by it: the last write for a key is the current value of that key. Last-write-wins is not a compromise here, it is the semantics; git does it with refs and an LSM tree does it with levels.

author: reek
body: Superseding is not deleting. The first edition of Colophon.codex is still in wi-works and still verifies, forever; it is simply no longer what the path points at. Removal is a separate act, and it wants a tombstone: see Authenticated Removal below, where it is built.

author: reek
body: This is also the reason DiskFacts' own in-memory index cannot serve: disk-load keys each fact by the hash of the stored LINE, not by the hash of the content that line describes. It is an index of records. This is an index of works.

author: reek
body: Superseding was never deleting, and neither is removal: a tombstone does not erase a fact, it records that a PATH is gone as of a point in the log. So the index reads definitions and tombstones together, in log order, and the last word for a path wins -- a definition puts the path in the tree, a later tombstone takes it out, a later definition puts it back. What none of this touches is wi-works: every edition ever stored is still addressable by its hash and still verifies, forever, tombstone or no. The tree forgets a path; the history does not forget a work.

author: reek
body: A tombstone's content is the path it retires. The path leaves wi-current (so no version is current) and leaves wi-paths (so a checkout does not walk it); wi-works is untouched.

author: reek
body: index-one in two halves, for a reader that must record an edition in the history without letting it decide the tree. index-works-add files the work by its hash and touches nothing else; index-tree-set points a path at a work and leaves the history alone.

author: reek
body: Give me this exact work, whatever the tree says today. A hash is a name that cannot go stale, which is the whole of why we address by them.

author: reek
body: Every path the store knows about, in the order it first heard of them. This is the tree, and it is the thing a checkout walks.

author: reek
body: A checkout is the whole of what a repository is for. Everything else -- the hashes, the signatures, the gate, the log -- exists so that this one function can hand you the source back and you can believe it.

author: reek
body: And it is a walk of the tree fetching each current work, which is exactly as dull as it should be. The interesting properties are not in this code, they are underneath it: the bytes came back byte-identical because they were content-addressed, the revised edition was taken and the superseded one left because the last write for a path is the current value of that path, and the whole thing verified because every work carries a signature the gate checks. A checkout that had to be clever would mean something below it was wrong.

author: reek
body: The result is the concatenation the compiler eats. That is not an accident of convenience: the point of it is that a program checked out of the store can be compiled and run, and the first one was.

author: reek
body: One work, checked out on its own. A checkout of the whole tree is this in a loop, and a checkout of nothing is honestly empty rather than absent.

author: reek
body: repo-index-from-disk reads every definition and tombstone the log holds and folds them, in order, into the tree and the history. It is correct and it is O(log): a store that has recorded a thousand editions replays a thousand editions on every boot, whether or not any of them is still current.

author: reek
body: A snapshot is the way out. It is one fact -- kind 40 -- carrying the whole materialized WorkIndex as of a point in the log: the tree (each live path and its current hash) and the history (every edition ever stored, so that a hash that is no longer current is still addressable, forever, which is the one property this store cannot lose). Rebuilding then means loading the snapshot and replaying only the entries written after it -- the tail -- instead of the whole log.

author: reek
body: Two things key a snapshot, and both are in the superblock. The COVERED HEAD is the log-head the snapshot was taken at; the tail is everything from there to the current head. The INDEX-GEN is bumped by compaction, which rewrites the log and moves every sector -- so a snapshot whose gen no longer matches the store describes sector positions that no longer mean what they did, and the rebuild falls back to a full replay rather than trust it. A snapshot is a cache that a full replay can always reconstruct; it is never the only copy of anything, because every fact it summarizes is still on the disk.

author: reek
body: The format is a header of four integers -- gen, covered-head, path-count, work-count -- then the body. The body is length-prefixed segments so that a path, a hash, or a source file full of pipes and newlines is taken verbatim by its length and never parsed for delimiters: first each (path, current-hash) pair, then each work as its SourceDefWire text. A segment is its character length, a pipe, then exactly that many characters.

author: reek
body: The whole materialized index as one text. The works come out of wi-works in no particular order, which is fine -- they are keyed by hash and the tree carries the order that matters.

author: reek
body: The generation, read on its own and cheaply, so a rebuild can decide whether a snapshot is worth parsing before it parses the whole thing.

author: reek
body: Take a snapshot of the index as it stands. The covered head is the current log-head -- everything on the disk right now -- captured before the snapshot fact is written, so the snapshot describes the log up to but not including itself. The kind-40 fact is not a definition or a tombstone, so a later rebuild's tail walk steps over it and folds only the real entries after it.

author: reek
body: The fast rebuild. With a snapshot whose generation still matches the store, load it and replay the tail; with none, or one stranded by a compaction, fall back to the full replay, which is always correct. The result is the same WorkIndex either way -- a snapshot is an optimization, never a source of truth.

author: reek
body: A definition is signed, and the gate can refuse one it does not trust. A tombstone was not: its content was the bare path it retired, so anyone who could write a sector could retire any path, and the tree honored it. Removal is an assertion like any other, and an unauthenticated assertion is exactly the hole the store exists to close.

author: reek
body: So a tombstone carries a signature now. It signs the path together with the author and the timestamp -- the same three things a definition's signature binds beyond its content hash -- so neither the path being retired nor its attribution can be altered without breaking the signature. The wire form is five pipe-delimited fields, path first; a line with fewer fields is a bare legacy tombstone, read as an unsigned removal of that path.

author: reek
body: Two indexes read the same log. repo-index-from-disk is TRUSTING: it honors every tombstone by its path, signed or not, resolving each path by log order, which is what the existing tree has always done and what the fast rebuild inherits. repo-index-verified is AUTHENTICATED, and it does two things the trusting index does not.

author: reek
body: First, it VERIFIES every assertion. A definition must hash to its own hash and carry a signature that verifies against a key the manifest holds at or above the threshold -- the same check the gate applies; a tombstone must verify the same way. An unsigned, forged, or untrusted definition or tombstone is dropped on the floor. Every verified edition still enters the history (addressable by hash forever); only verified assertions touch the tree.

author: reek
body: A definition verifies exactly as the gate verifies it: its content must hash to the hash it claims, and that hash, kind, author and timestamp must carry a signature from a key the manifest trusts at or above the threshold.

author: reek
body: A verified definition always enters the history; it takes the tree only if it is the newest thing said about its path.

author: reek
body: This used to live in SourceFactsBridge and sign "hash|path|quire|chapter" -- a sentence of its own invention, which no verifier in the tree knows how to check. The import gate verifies fact-signing-content: the content hash, the kind, the author and the timestamp. So that is what gets signed, and a definition signed here is one the gate can admit.

author: reek
body: The signature covers sd-hash, and sd-hash must address sd-content, or the gate's integrity guard refuses the fact before it ever looks at the signature. So the hash is recomputed here from the bytes we are about to store. A hash handed to us from outside is a claim about a file we did not read.

author: reek
body: Retire a path. The tombstone is a fact like any other -- appended, never overwriting -- whose content is the path it removes; the index reads it in log order and drops the path from the current tree.
